passages.t: Judah forsakes the law, and Shishak comes
passages.happening:
‘After Rehoboam had established his sovereignty and royal power, he and all Israel with him forsook the Law of the LORD’ (verse 1). ‘In the fifth year of Rehoboam’s reign, because they had been unfaithful to the LORD, Shishak king of Egypt came up and attacked Jerusalem’ (verse 2), with chariots, horsemen and troops from Libya, Sukkiim and Cush, and takes the fortified cities of Judah (verses 3-4).

Shemaiah the prophet comes to Rehoboam and the leaders with God's word: ‘You have forsaken Me; therefore, I have forsaken you into the hand of Shishak’ (verse 5). The leaders and the king humble themselves and say, “The LORD is righteous” (verse 6). God answers through Shemaiah that he will not destroy them, ‘Nevertheless, they will become his servants, so that they may learn the difference between serving Me and serving the kings of other lands’ (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 11 ended with three good years. This chapter sets the pattern the Chronicler uses for every king after: faithfulness brings strength, strength tempts a king to forget God, unfaithfulness brings trouble, and humbling oneself before God brings mercy. The sequence is plain: established, forsook, invaded, warned, humbled, spared. Scholars call this the Chronicler's theology of immediate retribution, because the results show within a king's own reign.

Shishak is the pharaoh known from Egyptian sources as Sheshonq I, founder of Egypt's Twenty-second Dynasty, of Libyan descent. His invasion is one of the earliest events in the history of the kings that can be tied to an outside record. On a wall of the temple of Amun at Karnak he left a relief listing many towns in Canaan he claimed to have subdued, and a fragment of a stela with his name was found at Megiddo. The campaign is usually dated about 925 BC. Jerusalem does not appear among the names that survive on the damaged Karnak list; many think Rehoboam's payment from the treasuries explains why the city was not destroyed.

The verbs carry the meaning. Forsake, azav, mirrors: they left the LORD, and he left them to Shishak. Humble, kana, comes four times and is the chapter's hinge, the same word as in 7:14. And serve, avodah, can mean both the worship of God and forced work for a human master. Judah would learn by comparison which was lighter.
passages.later: Solomon's prayer had asked for this: ‘and when they return to You with all their heart and soul in the land of the enemies who took them captive’ (2 Chronicles 6:38). A proverb says, ‘Pride goes before destruction, and a haughty spirit before a fall’ (Proverbs 16:18).
passages.hard:
Does the Chronicler teach that every disaster is punishment for a specific sin?

Chronicles often ties a king's faithfulness to good and his unfaithfulness to trouble within his own reign, and this chapter is a clear case. Some readers take it as a general rule for how God governs history. Most interpreters note that the Chronicler is writing about the covenant king and people of Judah, where the prophets explicitly interpret events, as Shemaiah does here. Other parts of Scripture, Job, many psalms, and Jesus' words about the tower of Siloam and the man born blind, warn against reading every suffering as a direct penalty. The Chronicler's pattern is best read as a call to his readers to seek God and humble themselves, not as a formula for diagnosing anyone else's troubles.

Even here, humbling brought mercy, not greatness. Judah was spared, and still served Egypt.
passages.asks: The king and the leaders said, The LORD is righteous, and God heard them. Ask what it would sound like for you to say that honestly about your own failures. And ask what you have learned about the difference between serving God and serving the powers around you.

passages.t: Gold shields for bronze, and Rehoboam's verdict
passages.happening:
Shishak takes the treasures of the temple and the palace, ‘including the gold shields that Solomon had made’ (verse 9). ‘Then King Rehoboam made bronze shields in their place’ (verse 10), and whenever the king goes to the house of the LORD the guards carry them and then return them to the guardroom (verse 11). ‘Because Rehoboam humbled himself, the anger of the LORD turned away from him, and He did not destroy him completely. Indeed, conditions were good in Judah’ (verse 12).

Rehoboam reigns seventeen years in Jerusalem, ‘the city the LORD had chosen from all the tribes of Israel in which to put His Name’ (verse 13); his mother is Naamah the Ammonite. ‘And Rehoboam did evil because he did not set his heart to seek the LORD’ (verse 14). There is war between Rehoboam and Jeroboam all their days (verse 15).
passages.hearers:
Solomon's golden age ends in a very visible way. The gold ceremonial shields, symbols of wealth carried in royal processions, go to Egypt, and bronze ones take their place. The ceremony goes on, while showing how much has been lost, and the detail that the guards carefully put the bronze back after each use has a touch of irony.

The closing notice follows the pattern Chronicles uses for every king: age, length of reign, mother, verdict, sources, burial. Naamah was an Ammonite, from east of the Jordan, and Solomon had married women from among them; Solomon's heir was half Ammonite. The verdict explains the whole reign: he did not set his heart to seek the LORD. The parallel in 1 Kings 14:25-28 records the invasion and the shields; Chronicles adds the army's size, Shemaiah's prophecy and the king's repentance.
passages.later: First Kings tells it in brief: ‘He took everything, including all the gold shields that Solomon had made’ (1 Kings 14:26).
passages.asks: Rehoboam humbled himself once, but he never set his heart to seek the LORD. Ask whether your turning to God is a moment in a crisis or the set of your heart. And ask what bronze you have put in place of gold and kept polishing as if nothing were lost.
